newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway may invest oil wealth in overseas stock.
newsitem.headline: Norway may invest oil wealth in overseas stock.

text.p: Norway, the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia, said on Tuesday it may pump 30 to 50 percent of the State Petroleum Fund into overseas stock exchanges.

The finance ministry said the fund may grow to about 425 billion crowns ($59.7 billion) by the end of 2001 from today's level of 50 billion crowns, or to over 30 percent of gross domestic product from five percent today.

"We are not going to put all our eggs in one basket, such as bonds, but we will spread the risk," Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg told a news conference. "We are proposing to open for investment in shares from January 1, 1998, to get lower risk and higher yield."
Norway, which has run up a budget surplus for three consecutive years thanks to its oil wealth, has so far invested the surplus in low-risk foreign government bonds only.
But the central bank had recommended that the fund portfolio be broadened to include equities in order to give a more stable long-term return.
"It is the preliminary assessment of the Ministry of Finance that the share of equities in the first years should be in the range of 30 to 50 percent," the ministry said in a statement.
It said a final decision on a new investment strategy for the fund would be made in the autumn.
Stoltenberg said: "Shares are seen as more risky than bonds. This is not quite true. It is true if you look at the annual swings. But it levels out over time."
"On a 20-year horizon we have never had a negative yield on shares, but we have had it on bonds," he said, showing charts with international yield statistics dating back to 1802.
Stoltenberg said the government may not start tapping the fund for domestic expenditure for the next 20 years or so.
"First of all, we are not so concerned about annual swings in the investments. Secondly, We are not so concerned about swings in the Norwegian currency," he said.

"This is an uncertain forecast and it works both ways," he said, commenting on the projected growth of the fund. "There could be more and there could be less money. The uncertainty on revenue is linked to production of oil and gas, the price of oil and gas and the foreign exchange rate. It also depends on what fiscal policy we pursue."

Norway's offshore platforms pump more than three million barrels of oil per day and daily output is expected to peak at 3.7 million barrels in the year 2000, declining to 2.8 million in 2005, according to the energy ministry.
Recoverable oil reserves are expected to last 14 years. The equivalent figure for natural gas -- Norway is a major gas exporter to continental Europe -- is 80 years.
Norway is setting aside the annual budget surplus in the petroleum fund as a buffer against sudden fluctuations in oil prices and as a guarantee for future pensions for its citizens.
The fund is being managed by the central bank, which invests in overseas paper only to avoid overheating the domestic economy. This policy will not be changed.
"We will invest on a few big recognised stock exchanges such as London, New York, Paris, Copenhagen and Stockholm," Stoltenberg said.
The petroleum fund's share portfolio will include many companies rather than a few big blue chips, he said.
"The risk is greater if you pick a few companies only," he said.
He said the central bank would continue to manage the fund and select brokerages which would help invest the money.

"We have to select the best and measure them against each other. We are talking about billions of crowns for Norwegian pensioners and Norwegian welfare. So we have to be professional in picking managers."
